Subject:   Case M.12278 – PARAMOUNT SKYDANCE / WARNER BROS
       DISCOVERY
         Commission decision pursuant to Article 6(1)(b) of Council Regulation
        No 139/2004 (1) and Article 57 of the Agreement on the European Economic
         Area (2)


Dear Sir or Madam,

(1)    On 2 June 2026, the European Commission received  notification of a proposed
        concentration pursuant to Article 4 of the Merger Regulation by which Paramount
       Skydance Corporation (‘Paramount’ or the ‘Notifying Party’, United States) intends to
        acquire  sole  control of Warner Bros. Discovery (‘Warner’, United  States)  (the
        ‘Transaction’). (3) Paramount and Warner are designated hereinafter as the ‘Parties’.




(1)     OJ L 24, 29.1.2004, p. 1 (the ‘Merger Regulation’). With effect from 1 December 2009, the Treaty on the
        Functioning of the European Union (‘TFEU’) has introduced certain changes, such as the replacement of
       ‘Community’ by ‘Union’ and ‘common market’ by ‘internal market’. The terminology of the TFEU will be
        used throughout this decision.
(2)     OJ L 1, 3.1.1994, p. 3 (the ‘EEA Agreement’).
(3)    OJ C 3264, 17.6.2026.

1.    THE PARTIES
(2)    Paramount is a US publicly listed global media, streaming and entertainment company
         that creates content and experiences for audiences worldwide, including films, television
          series, and animated content. Paramount’s portfolio of brands and production assets
         include, among others, Paramount Pictures, Paramount Television, CBS, CBS News,
      CBS Sports, Nickelodeon, MTV, BET, Comedy Central, Showtime, Paramount+, Pluto
     TV and Skydance Media, LLC animation, interactive/games and sports divisions. In
        2025, Paramount generated worldwide turnover of EUR 25.6 billion, of which EUR
          [details of the Parties’ revenues] billion in the EEA.
(3)    Warner is a US publicly listed global media, streaming and entertainment company that
         creates and distributes a diverse portfolio of content and products across television, film,
        streaming and interactive gaming. Warner’s portfolio of brands and production assets
         includes, among others, Discovery Channel, CNN, DC Studios, New Line Cinema, TNT
         Sports, Eurosport, Max, HBO, Warner Bros. Motion Picture Group, Warner Bros.
        Television Group, and Warner Bros. Games. In 2025, Warner generated worldwide
        turnover of EUR 33 billion, of which EUR [details of the Parties’ revenues] billion in the
      EEA.

2.    THE OPERATION AND CONCENTRATION
(4)    On 27 February 2026, Paramount and Warner executed a merger agreement pursuant to
       which Paramount will acquire all the shares in Warner for a cash consideration of
        approximately USD 110 billion (at a price of USD 31 per share). If the Transaction has
        not closed by 30 September 2026, Warner’s shareholders will receive a USD 0.25 per
        share ‘ticking fee’ for each quarter (measured daily) until closing.
(5)    As a result of the Transaction, Paramount will acquire sole control over Warner. The
        Transaction constitutes a concentration within the meaning of Article 3(1)(b) Merger
        Regulation.

3.    UNION DIMENSION
(6)     The undertakings concerned have a combined aggregate worldwide turnover of more
        than EUR 5 000 million (Paramount: EUR 25.6 billion; Warner: EUR 33 billion). Each
        of them has an EU-wide turnover in excess of EUR 250 million (Paramount: EUR [details
        of the Parties’ revenues] billion; Warner: EUR [details of the Parties’ revenues] billion),
       and neither of them achieves more than two-thirds of its aggregate EU-wide turnover
        within the same Member State. The notified operation therefore has a Union dimension.

4.    INDUSTRY OVERVIEW
(7)     The audiovisual (‘AV’) industry has traditionally been split into: (i) the theatrical value
         chain, centred on feature films and cinema exhibition, and (ii) the AV value chain,
        focused on television and home entertainment. Content is distributed in each of the
          theatrical and AV value chains, along three different levels: the upstream, intermediate
       and downstream. Many operators are vertically integrated and active at more than one
          level.
(8)     Theatrical value chain. The upstream level encompasses the production of films
        intended for theatrical release and the licensing of those films for exploitation in cinemas,
         regardless of whether the producer distributes the film itself or licenses the distribution
         rights to a third-party distributor. The intermediate level covers the wholesale distribution

                                                             2

of films to cinemas, carried out either by independent third-party distributors, or through
         self-distribution by film producers. The downstream  level includes the  theatrical
         exhibition of films by cinemas.
(9)   AV value chain. The upstream level encompasses the production of content (e.g. series,
     TV shows) and the licensing-out of such content to companies active in the intermediate
         or downstream levels. The intermediate level covers the wholesale supply of TV channels
         to retail TV distributors. The downstream level includes the retail provision of AV
         services to end-customers primarily via (i) linear TV channels, and (ii) subscription
        video-on-demand platforms (‘SVOD’).
(10)    The market for AV content constitutes the upstream level of the AV value chain,
       encompassing both the production of AV content and the licensing of distribution rights
         to wholesale suppliers of TV channels, as well as retail providers of AV services. At this
         level of the AV value chain, production studios either produce new AV content
       commissioned and tailored to the needs of other market participants, or license-out pre-
       produced AV content which is available off-the-shelf. (4)
(11)    The wholesale supply of TV channels constitutes the intermediate level between the
        upstream creation and licensing of AV content and the downstream retail distribution of
     AV content to end customers. At this level, wholesalers package AV content and
         associated broadcasting  rights  into  linear and non-linear  offerings  for  retail TV
          distributors. (5)
(12)    The retail provision of AV services to end users constitutes the downstream level of the
     AV value chain which follows the upstream level for the production and licensing of AV
        content and the intermediate level for wholesale supply of TV channels. Retail suppliers
         of AV content include (i) TV distributors, including Multichannel Video Programming
         Distributors (‘MVPDs’), (ii) Over The Top (‘OTT’) providers delivering AV content
         online, and (iii) to a limited extent, in physical formats. (6)
(13)    The AV value chain has been undergoing a significant structural change over the last
         years, as linear viewership is shifting towards non-linear services, especially SVOD
         services. The changing media consumption patterns have resulted in a decline in linear
     TV viewership and a corresponding  increase  in  non-linear consumption  of AV
         content. (7)
(14)    The Parties are active on all levels of the theatrical and AV value chains except for
          theatrical exhibition (as they do not operate their own cinemas).

5.    RELEVANT MARKETS

5.1.    Introduction
(15)    The Parties’ activities result in horizontal overlaps that give rise to affected markets in
           (i) the production and licensing of films for theatrical release, (ii) the distribution of films
         for theatrical release, (iii) the production and licensing of AV content, (iv) the wholesale
        supply of TV channels, and (v) the retail supply of AV services. (8) (9)
(16)    The Transaction also results in vertical relationships between the Parties’ business
          activities in some levels of the theatrical value chain and in some levels of the AV value
         chain. However, these vertical links do not give rise to affected markets in any EEA
         country. (10)
(17)     Further, the Transaction results in conglomerate links in light of the Parties’ activities in
        neighbouring markets in the AV value chain where the Parties’ market share is 30% or
        more.

5.2.    Production and licensing of films for theatrical release
(18)    Both Parties are active in the production and licensing of films for theatrical release.
(19)    Paramount is active in the production and licensing of films for theatrical release through
         the following studios and labels:

(9)     The Transaction results in affected markets only in the market for retail supply of SVOD services and no
         affected markets within any other sub-segmentations of the market for the retail supply of AV services.
(10)     For completeness, this decision will discuss the vertical link between the production and licensing of AV
         content (upstream) and retail supply of SVOD services (downstream).

5.2.1.   Product market definition

5.2.1.1. Commission precedents
(21)    In previous decisions, the Commission has considered the question whether the
        production and licensing of films for theatrical release and the distribution of films for
          theatrical release constitute a single or two separate product markets. While in some cases
         the definition of the market was ultimately left open (15), in others the Commission found
         that the production/licensing and the distribution of films for theatrical release constitute
       two separate markets. (16)

      Woman and the Flash.

(22)    In   particular,  in  Time  Warner/CME,  the  Commission  considered   that  the
         production/licensing of films for theatrical distribution and the distribution of these films
         for theatrical release constitute two separate product markets. (17)
(23)   More  recently,  in  The  Walt  Disney  Company/Twenty-First  Century  Fox  and
      Amazon/MGM, the Commission defined two separate product markets: one for the
        production and licensing of distribution rights to third-party distributors, and one for the
         distribution of films to cinemas. (18) The Commission noted that simply producing a film
        cannot constitute a market before a market-based exchange, such as the distribution of a
         film, takes place. (19)
(24)    The Commission has also considered – but left open – a further segmentation of the
        market between films produced by US film studios (hereafter also referred to as ‘US
         films’) and those produced by non-US film studios (hereafter also referred to as ‘non-US
          films’). (20)

5.2.1.2. The Notifying Party’s views
(25)    The Notifying Party does not express a view in the Form CO as regards the existence of
        a market for the production and licensing of films that would differ from the production
       and licensing of films to third-party distributors, as discussed in Amazon/MGM and The
       Walt Disney Company/Twenty-First Century Fox. (21)

5.2.1.3. Commission’s assessment
(26)    The Commission found that while there are fully integrated film studios that produce and
         distribute their own content, not all content producers are distributors. Similarly, there
         are independent distributors that do not produce content, but operate solely at the
         distribution level, engaging directly with cinemas where the content producers are either
        unable or unwilling to do so. (22) Having regard to the above, the Commission concludes
         that production and licensing on the one hand, and distribution of films for theatrical
         release, on the other hand, belong to separate relevant markets.
(27)   As regards a possible further sub-segmentation between US and non-US films, from a
       demand side most cinema operators consider that films by non-US film studios are never
         alternatives to films by US film studios. (23) This is because, as a general matter, films
       from non-US studios do not generate the same level of admissions, box-office revenue
         or footfall as films from US studios, with the latter typically accounting for a vast
        majority of admissions. (24) Further, it appears from the market investigation that films
       from US studios generally benefit from greater public recognition and substantially larger
        marketing budgets. (25) Finally, it follows from the market investigation that US studios
        obtain better commercial terms in their negotiations with cinema operators than non-US

        element of  differentiation  that  will be considered  in the competitive assessment
        (paragraphs (201) and (210) and Table 2).

5.2.1.4. Conclusion
(29)    In light of the above, the Commission considers that, for the purposes of this decision,
         the production and licensing of films for theatrical release and the distribution of films
         for theatrical release constitute two separate product markets.
(30)    The question whether the market for the production and licensing of films for theatrical
         release should be further segmented based on whether the films were produced by US or
       non-US studios can be left open, since the Transaction does not raise serious doubts as
         to its compatibility with the internal market under any plausible market definition.
(31)    The Commission will assess the impact of the Transaction on the narrower market
        segment, i.e., the market for the production and licensing of US films for theatrical
         release, since the Parties are not active in the production and licensing of non-US films.

5.2.2.   Geographic market definition

5.2.2.1. Commission precedents
(32)    In past decisions, the Commission found the geographic market for the production and
         licensing of films for theatrical release to likely be at least EEA-wide and possibly
        worldwide. (28)

5.2.2.2. The Notifying Party’s views
(33)   As explained at paragraph (25) above, the Notifying Party does not express a view in the
       Form CO as regards the existence of a market for the production and licensing of films,
         nor, therefore, on its geographic scope. (29)

(27)     European Commission, Directorate-General for Communications Networks, Content and Technology, ‘The
       European Media Industry Outlook 2025’, Figure 25, page 45. On the basis of European Audiovisual
        Observatory data, films of US origin accounted for 66% of cinema admissions in the Union in 2023, national
        European films for 23%, European films originating in another European country for 6%, and films of other
         origin for 5%. These figures are compiled by origin of the work rather than by the origin of the producing

5.2.2.3. Commission’s assessment
(34)    Most responding film studios, and all responding US film studios, consider that they
       compete with one another on a worldwide level, including in the EEA. (30) As also
        explained by several respondents to the market investigation that expressed a view
        (‘respondents’), studios compete globally for financing, screenplays and talent, as well
        as for audiences in cinemas. (31) No responding studio considered that US studios and
       non-US studios do not compete with one another. (32)
(35)    The Commission acknowledges that studios frequently license the theatrical rights to
          their films to third-party distributors on a territory-by-territory basis, and that respondents
        pointed in this regard to the need for marketing and versioning to reflect local linguistic
       and cultural specificities. (33) However, respondents explained that sub-distributors are
       engaged where the studio does not have a local presence capable of serving a fragmented
         national exhibition market. (34) The territorial scope of the licences granted therefore
          reflects the organisation of the downstream distribution of films to exhibitors, which is
         national in scope (Section 5.3), rather than the conditions of competition prevailing at the
        upstream level. The choice of the territories for which rights are granted is itself a
       commercial parameter determined by the studio, and the studios from which distributors
         in any given Member State source films are the same across the EEA. The Commission
         therefore considers that territorial licensing does not evidence national conditions of
        competition for the production and licensing of films for theatrical release from US
         studios.
(36)   Some respondents indicated that competition also takes place at national or regional
          level. Several non-US studios explained that, in the territories in which they are active,
        they compete with local producers as well as with US studios and with producers active
         in several countries. (35) One US studio likewise explained that, alongside worldwide
        competition between major studios, local and regional producers compete for local-
        language and culturally specific content. (36) These responses concern the production of
         local and local-language films. They are consistent with the segmentation retained in
        Section 5.2.1, and explain why the geographic scope of this market was left open in past
         decisions, which concerned an undifferentiated market encompassing both films from
      US studios and locally produced films. That consideration bears on the market for films
       from non-US studios and not on the market for films from US studios.

5.2.2.4. Conclusion
(37)    In light of the above, the Commission considers that, for the purposes of this decision,
         the geographic market for the production and licensing of US films for theatrical release
           is at least EEA-wide. It will therefore carry out the assessment of this market on an EEA-
       wide basis.

5.3.     Distribution of films for theatrical release
(38)    Both Parties are active in the distribution of films for theatrical release.
(39)    Paramount self-distributes theatrical films to cinemas directly in France, Ireland and

5.3.1.   Product market definition

5.3.1.1. Commission precedents
(45)    In previous decisions, the Commission has considered the question of whether the
        production and licensing and distribution of films for theatrical release constitute a single
         or two separate product markets. While in some cases the definition of the market was
         ultimately  left open (40), in others the Commission found that the production and
         licensing, on the one hand, and the distribution of films for theatrical release, on the other
        hand, constitute two separate markets. (41)

5.3.1.2. The Notifying Party’s views
(46)    For the reasons set out below, the Notifying Party submits that a distinction between self-
         distribution of films for theatrical release and the licensing thereof to third-party
         distributors is not warranted.
(47)   From a supply side, studios routinely choose between self-distribution and licensing to
         third-party distributors on a territory-by-territory basis. In practice, a studio may directly
         distribute in some countries while appointing a third-party distributor in other countries
         or may change distribution partners from time to time. Also, distribution agreements
         typically involve revenue-sharing arrangements (e.g., distribution fees as a share of total
       box office), aligning incentives across the value chain, recognizing the inherent risky

nature of film production and distribution, and reflecting economic integration rather than
         separation.
(48)   From a demand side, first, cinemas seek timely access to titles that will draw audiences.
        Their decisions turn on expected title performance, not on whether a title is distributed
         directly by a studio or via a licensed  distributor. Second, cinemas apply similar
         negotiating criteria, commitments and revenue-splits whether dealing with a studio
         directly or with a licensed distributor, which typically handles the studio’s entire slate in
        a given territory. Third, booking and programming decisions by cinemas respond to the
       same commercial considerations whether they contract directly with a studio or with a
         licensed distributor. (42)
(49)    The Notifying Party also considers a potential segmentation between films produced by
      US studios and those produced by non-US studios unwarranted, for the following
         reasons:
(50)   From the supply-side perspective, US and non-US studios compete in similar ways, for
        example, releasing films theatrically and using marketing to raise awareness of a new
         release across the EEA. Further, co-productions and financing partnerships between US
       and non-US studios are common and further blur any line between US and non-US films.
(51)   From the demand-side perspective, first, the film industry is inherently global. US and
       non-US films generally compete for the same audience and screen time, with cinemas
         curating diverse slates and distributors (including local ones) handling films from both
      US and non-US studios. Second, audience demand is primarily driven by story, genre,
          cast, rather than the geographic location of the film studio that produced the film. Third,
          ticket prices at cinemas do not depend on whether a film is produced by a US or non-US
         studio, demonstrating that consumers view these films as interchangeable. Fourth, box
         office depends on factors such as quality and marketing spend rather than whether the
        film originates from a US vs. non-US studio. Fifth, reviews and critical acclaim – which
         influence consumer choice – are evaluated without regard to production origin. (43)
(52)    In any event, the Notifying Party submits that the precise market definition can be left
        open, as the Transaction does not raise serious doubts as to its compatibility with the
         internal market under any plausible market definition. (44)

5.3.1.3. Commission’s assessment
(53)    Most studios and distributors that responded to the Commission’s market investigation
        consider that there is a separate market for the distribution of films to cinemas. (45).
         Further, the Commission considers that it would be artificial to segment this market per
         distribution route, that is distribution either directly by film studios or through licenses
        granted to third-party distributors. In this respect the Commission also notes that in both

(68)    The Notifying Party submits that the production and supply of commissioned AV content

         acquirers of AV content operate a unified content budget and continuously arbitrate
       between in-house production, co-production, commissioning and licensing based on slate
        needs, editorial strategy, timing, exclusivity and expected return on investment, with
        audience demand driven by whether content is new to the viewer rather than by its mode
         of acquisition. (62) The Notifying Party further notes that the industry has shifted towards
         greater content ownership, further blurring the boundary between in-house production,
        commissioning and acquisition of pre-produced content. (63)

         industry. This is because the popularity of linear TV is in sustained decline as linear
        consumption is shifting at scale to non-linear viewing alternatives, mainly SVOD/VOD
         services. SVOD/VOD services are now routinely promoted and offered by retail TV
        distributors/MVPDs  alongside  linear TV  channel  portfolios.  Equally,  retail TV
        distributors/MVPDs increasingly integrate, and weigh SVOD/VOD offers in wholesale
         carriage negotiations. As a result, the delineation of a relevant product market including

         acquisition of TV channels often cover both FTA TV and pay TV channel portfolios;

(100)   Further, the Notifying Party submits that a distinction of pay TV channels between
       ‘premium’ and ‘basic’ would not be appropriate. There is no industry-wide definition as
         to what constitutes ‘premium’ and ‘basic’. The distinction is further blurred due to the
          rise of bundled packages. From a supply side perspective, channel programming sits on
        a continuum of quality. The same TV channel may be re-tiered or repositioned across
          retail TV distributors/MVPDs, further undermining any split. From a demand side
         perspective, retail TV distributors/MVPDs build channel lineups to meet audience
        preferences for variety, quality, and convenience. They substitute among channels based
       on price, audience appeal and terms. For viewers, the value is the overall bundle and
        experience, including the ability to access diverse content via a single subscription. (98)
(101)   In addition, the Notifying Party submits that a distinction by genre is not warranted. From
        a supply side perspective, wholesale suppliers of TV channels typically package channels
         of different genres together and negotiate them with retail TV distributors/MVPDs using
         the same commercial levers  (e.g., carriage  fees, minimum guarantees, marketing
        commitments). Wholesale negotiations are typically conducted on a portfolio basis
         (including multiple TV channels and VOD content) rather than on channel-by-channel
         basis or genre‑by‑genre basis, and often a single fee is charged across all channels in the
        package. From a demand side perspective, retail TV distributors/MVPDs routinely swap
     TV channels within and across genres. The retailers’ decision to acquire a particular
        channel does not turn on whether a channel could be identified as belonging to a
         particular ‘genre’. Retailers build diverse bundles of channels across different genres to
         offer consumers a wide selection of content in one subscription. Therefore, they buy
         portfolios, not isolated genre silos, and carriage negotiations occur on ratings and brand
        equity rather than genre. (99)
(102)   Last, the Notifying Party notes that a segmentation between linear and non-linear services
        does not reflect market dynamics as much of the same content is available in both linear
       and non-linear form. Most retail suppliers of AV services acquire both linear and non-
         linear rights together (e.g., linear rights plus non-linear rights such as TV Everywhere
       and catch-up services), rather than purchasing them separately. Similarly, the majority of
        wholesale suppliers supply both linear and non-linear rights to retailers of AV services
        (with most wholesale TV channel licencing agreements including non-linear catch-up
       and catalogue rights as standard). (100)

5.5.1.4. Conclusion
(121)   In light of the above, the Commission considers that, for the purposes of this decision, it
           is not appropriate to consider a potential segmentation in the market for the wholesale
        supply of TV channels between linear and non-linear services. In what concerns all other
         potential segmentations, the Commission considers that the precise product market
         definition for the wholesale supply of TV channels may be left open, as the Transaction
        does not raise serious doubts as to its compatibility with the internal market under any
         potential product market definition. For the purposes of this decision, the Commission
        conducted  a  competitive  assessment  considering  each  of  the  potential  market
        segmentations presented above (i.e., distinction between FTA and pay TV channels,

5.6.1.2. The Notifying Party’s views
(131)   The Notifying Party submits that the market definition can be  left open, as the
        Transaction does not raise any competitive concerns on any potential plausible market.
       However, the Parties note that linear services exert a declining competitive pressure on
         non-linear services, particularly on SVOD services. (136)
(132)   In particular, the Notifying Party submits that SVOD services are not substitutable with
         linear television and other non-linear services, such as advertising-funded video-on-
       demand (‘AVOD’),  transactional video-on-demand (‘TVOD’), PPV and  free ad-
        supported streaming television (‘FAST’). (137)
(133)    First, the Notifying Party submit that, from a supply perspective, the SVOD services
        business model differs fundamentally from linear television, which offers scheduled
       programming, and from non-linear retail services like AVOD, TVOD, and PPV services,
       which  rely on  different  monetization models,  offer a  different consumer  value
         proposition, and exhibit different consumption patterns. These differences translate into
          distinct pricing structures, content strategies and investment incentives. (138)
(134)   Second, from a demand perspective, SVOD services provide on-demand access to
        content libraries across devices and are primarily based on subscription revenues,
        whereas linear television is based on scheduled programming and is often oriented
        towards live content, including news and sports. (139)
(135)   Third, SVOD services are not constrained by AVOD and FAST services, given the
        absence of a subscription fee and the presence of ads. SVOD users may complement their
        viewing experiences with AVOD/FAST services but would not generally replace their
     SVOD subscriptions with ad-funded free alternatives. (140)
(136)   Fourth, SVOD services also differ from TVOD and PPV services, which are based on
        one-off transactions for individual  titles or specific events (often live) rather than
         recurring subscriptions. TVOD/PPV viewers will not typically expand one-off purchases
         into recurring subscription fees absent a broader change in viewing needs. (141)
(137)    Finally, the Notifying Party submits that video sharing platforms and user generated
        platforms like YouTube, TikTok or Instagram, are not substitutes for SVOD services.
       Most content on those services is user generated, not commissioned or overseen. That is
        a stark difference from the highly produced, scripted, longform programming that drives
     SVOD subscriptions. (142)

        supply of SVOD services, the Commission’s market investigation focused on whether

         the relevant geographic market for the retail supply of AV services, including all its
         possible sub-segments (including SVOD), is national in scope.

6.    COMPETITIVE ASSESSMENT

6.1.    Introduction
(147)   Under Article 2(2) and (3) of the Merger Regulation, the Commission must assess
        whether a proposed concentration would significantly impede effective competition in
         the internal market or in a substantial part of it, in particular through the creation or
        strengthening of a dominant position.
(148)   In this respect, a merger may entail horizontal and/or non-horizontal (namely, vertical or
        conglomerate) effects. Horizontal effects are those deriving from a concentration where
         the undertakings concerned are actual or potential competitors of each other in one or
       more of the relevant markets concerned. Vertical effects are those deriving from a
        concentration where the undertakings concerned are active on different levels of the
        supply chain. Conglomerate effects are those deriving from a concentration where the
        undertakings concerned are in a relationship which is neither horizontal nor vertical. A
        concentration may involve all three types of effects. In such a case, the Commission will
         appraise horizontal and non-horizontal effects in accordance with the guidance set out in

6.2.    Rationale of the Transaction
(149)   The Notifying Party submits that the Transaction will enable the merged entity to reach
       more consumers, increase output and compete more effectively across streaming, filmed
         entertainment, and television media.
(150)   In streaming, the merged  entity will provide a broader platform offering across
        Paramount+, HBO Max, Discovery+, and Pluto TV (Free Ad-Supported Streaming
         Television, ‘FAST’), which has the required scale to effectively compete with Netflix,
         the dominant SVOD incumbent. Paramount intends on creating a scaled streaming
        platform by integrating Paramount+ and HBO Max and plans to increase content spend.
(151)   In filmed entertainment, the merged entity will maintain the studios as distinct creative
         organisations, growing the scaled supply of high-quality content for their combined
         services and third-party distribution. Post-Transaction, Paramount expects studios’
        revenues to grow as the merged entity’s combined film slate (154) increases to [>30] films
        with larger average worldwide box office estimates [details of the Parties’ strategy and
        business activities] and growth in the TV licensing to third parties [details of the Parties’
         strategy and business activities]. In television media, the Transaction brings together
        Paramount’s and Warner’s complementary content across linear broadcasting and will
         offer a more compelling proposition to advertisers.
(152)   The Notifying Party further submits that the merged entity will operate on a more than
     USD 6 billion cost synergy opportunity, in addition to the more than USD 3 billion in
        standalone cost efficiencies that Paramount expects to achieve in its current internal
         transformational plans. These efficiencies will help the merged entity to compete against
        major industry players like Netflix and Disney. These cost savings opportunities will be
        generated in (i) labour, via the elimination of overlapping roles ([details of anticipated
         synergies]), (ii) non-labour savings, from overlapping non-labour spend in areas like
          [details of anticipated synergies] and (iii) [details of anticipated synergies]. (155)

6.4.    Horizontal effects

6.4.1.   Legal framework
(167)   The Horizontal Merger Guidelines describe two main ways in which horizontal mergers
      may significantly impede effective competition. In particular, the proposed concentration
        might be creating or strengthening a dominant position: (i) by eliminating important
        competitive constraints on one or more firms, which consequently would have increased
        market power, without resorting to coordinated behaviour (non-coordinated effects); and
            (ii) by changing the nature of competition in such a way that firms that previously were
        not coordinating their behaviour, are significantly more likely to coordinate and raise
         prices or otherwise harm effective competition (coordinated effects). (167)

6.4.1.1. Non-coordinated effects
(168)  A merger giving rise to horizontal non-coordinated effects might significantly impede
         effective competition by creating or strengthening the dominant position of a single firm,
       one which, typically, would have an appreciably larger market share than the next
        competitor post-merger. Moreover, also mergers that do not lead to the creation or the
        strengthening of a single firm’s dominant position may create competition concerns
        under the substantive  test set out in Article 2(2) and Article 2(3) of the Merger
        Regulation. Regarding mergers in oligopolistic markets, the Merger Regulation clarifies
         that ‘under certain circumstances, concentrations involving the elimination of important
        competitive constraints that the merging parties exerted upon each other, as well as a

(167)     Horizontal Merger Guidelines, paragraph 22.
                                                             40

reduction of competitive pressure on the remaining competitors, may, even in the absence
         of a likelihood of coordination between the members of the oligopoly, result in a
         significant impediment to effective competition’. (168)
(169)   The Horizontal Merger Guidelines list a number of factors which may influence whether
         or not significant horizontal non-coordinated effects are likely to result from a merger,
        such as the large market shares of the merging firms, the fact that the merging firms are
         close competitors, the limited possibilities for customers to switch suppliers, or the fact
         that the merger would eliminate an important competitive force. Not all those factors
       need to be present to make significant non-coordinated effects likely and it is not an
        exhaustive list. (169)
(170)   The Horizontal Merger Guidelines acknowledge that a merger that creates or strengthens
         the market power of a buyer may also significantly impede effective competition, in
         particular by creating or strengthening a dominant position. In certain circumstances,
        competition in the downstream markets could be adversely affected if, in particular, the
       merged entity was likely to use its buyer power vis-à-vis its suppliers to foreclose its
          rivals. (170)
(171)  To assess whether a merger that creates or strengthens buyer power would significantly
       impede effective competition, the Commission must analyse the competitive conditions
         in the upstream markets and to evaluate the possible positive and negative effects of the
        merger. (171)
(172)   In this context, paragraphs 24-36 of the Horizontal Merger Guidelines apply mutatis
        mutandis to the buyer side of the market, to investigate whether the Transaction would
          result in an increase in buyer power, as a result of the elimination of important
        competitive constraints that the merging Parties exerted upon each other prior to the
         Transaction.
(173)   These principles apply to all upstream purchasing markets, including markets for the
        purchase of labour. The Market Definition Notice applies to purchasing markets, with
         the substitution assessment focusing on the alternatives available to suppliers i.e., the
        workers. (172) Effects impacting workers but unrelated to the loss of competition resulting
       from the merger — such as corporate restructuring — fall outside the scope of this
        assessment under Article 2 of the Merger Regulation.

6.4.1.2. Coordinated effects
(174)  A merger in a concentrated market may also significantly impede effective competition
       due to horizontal coordinated effects where, through the creation or the strengthening of
        a dominant position, it increases the likelihood that firms are able to coordinate their
        behaviour and raise prices, even without entering into an agreement or resorting to a
        concerted practice within the meaning of Article 101 TFEU. A merger may also make
        coordination  easier, more  stable  or more  effective  for  firms  that were  already
        coordinating before the merger, either by making the coordination more robust or by
        permitting to coordinate on even higher prices. (173)

(175)  To assess whether a merger gives rise to horizontal coordinated effects, the Commission
        should examine, firstly, whether it would be possible to reach terms of coordination and,
        secondly, whether the coordination would likely be sustainable. These criteria are
        elaborated further below.
(176)  As regards the possibility of reaching terms of coordination, coordination is more likely
         to emerge in markets where it is relatively simple to reach a common understanding on
         the terms of coordination. (174) Coordination may take various forms, including keeping
         prices above the competitive level, limiting output or capacity, limiting product features,
        delaying innovation, or dividing the market, for instance by geographic area, by customer
         characteristics or by allocating contracts in bidding markets. Firms may also coordinate
       by following the market leader in its commercial strategy, such as a price increase or a
       change to other commercial or supply terms. (175)
(177)   Moreover,  in  examining  the  possibility  and  sustainability  of  coordination,  the
       Commission should specifically consider the changes that the Transaction brings about,
        focusing on whether those changes are likely to create or strengthen an environment
        conducive to coordination, rather than on establishing that coordination will actually
         occur. The reduction in the number of firms in a market may in itself be a factor that
          facilitates coordination. A merger may also increase the risk of coordinated effects in
         other ways, for example by eliminating a firm with a disruptive presence on the market,
       by increasing similarities between the remaining firms, or by creating structural or
       commercial links between competitors, including through joint ventures.
(178)  As regards the sustainability of coordination, coordination is sustainable where three
         further conditions are met, in addition to reaching a shared understanding on the terms of
         coordination. (176) Firstly, the coordinating undertakings must be able to monitor to a
         sufficient degree whether the terms of the coordination are being adhered to; there must
        be  sufficient market  transparency  for each undertaking concerned  to be aware,
         sufficiently precisely and quickly, of the way in which the market conduct of each of the
         other participants in the coordination is evolving. Secondly, there must be some form of
         credible deterrent mechanism that can come into play if deviation from the terms of
        coordination is detected. Thirdly, the reactions of outsiders, such as current or future
         competitors, and also the reactions of customers, should not be such as to jeopardise the
         results expected from the coordination. (177) In applying these conditions, it is necessary
         to avoid a mechanical approach involving the separate verification of each of them in
          isolation, without taking account of the overall economic mechanism of a hypothetical
          tacit coordination. (178)

6.4.3.   The theatrical distribution value chain - Assessment of unilateral effects
(183)  As set out in Sections 5.2 and 5.3 above, the Commission has previously found that
         separate markets exist for (i) the production and licensing of films for theatrical release,
       and (ii) the distribution of films to cinemas.
(184)   The impact of the Transaction on the market for the production and licensing of US films
         for theatrical release will be assessed in Section 6.4.3.1. The impact of the Transaction
       on the market  for the  distribution of US films  to cinemas  will be assessed  in
        Section 6.4.3.2. (183)

6.4.3.1. Production and licensing of US films for theatrical release

6.4.3.1.1     The Notifying Party’s views
(185)   The Notifying Party submits that the horizontal overlap between Paramount and Warner
         as regards the production and licensing of films for theatrical release will not lead to any
        competition concerns for the following reasons.
(186)    First, the Notifying Party submits that the rise of subscription streaming services and the
         entry of large technology companies into content production and distribution have
       expanded competition. As a result of this, the concepts of a ‘big five’ / ‘legacy’ studio
       would be outdated.
(187)   Second, the Notifying Party submits that the model by which studios distributed most of
          their films through cinemas, before turning to rental and other windows, has changed by
         the shift in audience consumption habits. According to the Notifying Party, streaming
        has surpassed cinemas in 2022 and many consumers now view new feature films on a
        small screen (e.g. TV, tablet) via streaming services.
(188)   Third, the Notifying Party submits that the dynamics in the market mean that no film
         studio can accumulate or sustain market power over time. Film performance is inherently
         uncertain, and  all films would be substitutable. According to the Notifying Party,
        competition takes place film-by-film and consumers do not base purchasing and viewing
         decisions based on the name of the studio. This is reflected in box office revenues of film
         studios, which are inherently volatile. (184)
(189)   In relation to complaints that the Transaction may result in a reduction of theatrical output
       by the Parties post-merger, the Notifying Party submits that the Transaction will not lead
         to any competition concerns for the following reasons.
(190)    Firstly, the Notifying Party submits that a hypothesis of a reduction in theatrical output
        does not accurately reflect the economics of the film industry. The Notifying Party argues

         in 1997) and A24 (founded in 2012) show that entry into the market for the production
       and supply of films for theatrical release is possible.
(214)   In the second place, several large tech companies that were active in adjacent markets
       have recently entered the market. Amazon acquired MGM in 2022. Apple founded Apple
        Studios in 2019 and has produced films for theatrical release since 2023.
(215)   In the third place, the Commission considers that while access to valuable IP (franchises)
           is the most important parameter to be successful, companies such as Apple and A24 show
         that successful entry without access to such IP is possible.
(216)   In the fourth place, the Commission tested in its market investigation whether vertical
         integration, that is, having one’s own distribution arm, is an important parameter to be
         successful. Film studios and distributors consider that vertical integration is a less
        important parameter for a film studio to be successful than the access to valuable IP, the

6.4.3.1.2.1.   Reduction of output
       During its investigation, the Commission received complaints from cinemas that the
        Transaction may result in a reduction of the number of films that the Parties would release
         in cinemas. For example, one cinema stated: (247) ‘Industry experience suggests that
        consolidation among major studios can lead to a reduction in overall theatrical output
        over time. For example, following the Disney-20th Century Fox transaction, the number
         of theatrical releases from the acquired studio significantly decreased compared to
         historical levels. A similar dynamic may occur in this case, although the extent and timing
         of any such effect remain uncertain’.
(217)   These concerns contradict the repeated public statements by Paramount to the opposite.
       During CinemaCon 2026, the largest annual industry gathering, its CEO stated in a
         presentation: ‘The second reason I came here today is I wanted to look every single one
         of you in the eye and give you my word: once we combine with Warner Bros., we are
        going to make a minimum of 30 films annually, across both studios. And every film –
        every film – will receive a full theatrical release, with a minimum 45-day window starting
        today’ (emphasis added). (248) In the first quarter Earnings Call for Paramount, its CEO
         similarly stated: ‘We are firmly committed to 30 theatrical films per year. If you look at
         the schedule, we have 15films [sic] on the calendar to release this year, up from 8 last
         year. So we’ve come close to basically doubling the output of our film studio, Paramount.
            If you look at the great job that the team at WBD has done, they have 15 films on the
         release calendar for this year. So the 2 companies are actually making 30 films to date,
       which Ithink [sic] is important to note and accelerating’ (emphasis added). (249)
(218)   Despite Paramount CEO’s public statements, and in light of the complaints it received,
         the Commission assesses whether the merged entity will have the incentive to reduce the
       number of films released as a result of the Transaction. (250)
(219)   While cinemas have expressed concerns that the Parties may reduce their combined film
        output following the proposed Transaction, the responses of film studios and distributors
         are more nuanced. While most of them indicated that the Parties have the incentive to do
         so, many were of the opposite view or considered that it would depend on the conditions
         of the merger. (251)
(220)   In view of the respondents’ replies, the Commission’s assessment focuses on the
        following elements: (i) Disney’s reduction of film output following its acquisition of
        Twenty-First Century Fox in 2019 (252); (ii) the fact that the merged entity would carry a
         significant amount of debt, which may force the Parties to reduce film output (253); and
            (iii) whether the combined current annual film output of Paramount and Warner would
        exceed what is economically optimal for the merged entity.

(221)    First, the Commission considers that Disney’s reduction of film output following its
         acquisition of Twenty-First Century Fox does not in itself constitute proof that the Parties
       would have the incentive to reduce film output following the Transaction.
(222)   In the first place, the Commission notes that Disney has a significantly different business
       model than the Parties. Disney is part of The Walt Disney Company. In addition to The
       Walt Disney Company’s entertainment business segment, which includes its activities in
         the theatrical distribution and AV value chains, a large part of The Walt Disney
       Company’s revenues is generated by the Parks, Experiences and Products business
       segment which includes its entertainment parks, cruise line and consumer products. (254)
        Hence, The Walt Disney Company has many more ways to monetize its IP than the
          Parties. As a result, the Parties are more dependent on film revenue than The Walt Disney
       Company.
(223)   In the second place, Disney’s acquisition of Twenty-First Century Fox had a different
        business rationale. As Bob Iger, Disney’s CEO at the time, explained, Disney evaluated
         the  acquisition ‘through the lens  of  [its]  future business’ with the objective of
         ‘accelerating [its] transformation into the DTC space on a global basis’. To achieve this,
       Disney intended to use Fox’s content library to ‘further enrich the content mix on [its]
     DTC platforms’ and refocus Fox’s studios on producing films for theatrical release as
        well as for Disney+ and Hulu. (255).
(224)   In the third place, the acquisition of Twenty-First Century Fox in 2019 was followed by
         the Covid-19 pandemic and later by the US writers’ strike in 2023. This has influenced
         the output of US films in general but also had an influence on the production and release
         strategies of said studios. These two exogeneous shocks make it hard to isolate any
         potential merger-driven reduction in theatrical output.
(225)    Firstly, the Covid-19 pandemic had a consequential negative impact on the industry for
        a significant period, as regards both film shootings and their release in cinemas, given
         the strict rules that applied in terms of masks, vaccination and social distancing. When
         studios were recovering from the adverse impacts of the pandemic, they were hit by the
         industry strikes in 2023. These have impacted all film studios, including Disney.
(226)   Secondly, the Commission notes that the Covid-19 pandemic also resulted in Disney
        deciding to release certain films directly on its streaming platform, which was launched
         in late 2019 and early 2020, depending on the market. In this regard, it is important to
        note that Disney has a significantly stronger position in the retail supply of SVOD
         services than the Parties, as set out in paras. (454) and (459) below. More importantly,
       Disney has reversed course after the Covid-19 pandemic. As noted by UNIC, ‘Disney is
        committed to theatrical releases, and while it released its films directly on its streaming
         service Disney+ during COVID-19, now the release of their new films starts with an
         exclusive theatrical window in cinemas’ (256).
(227)   Thirdly, the considerations set out above make  it difficult to isolate and assess any
         potential merger-driven reduction in output, as any observed reduction could equally
          reflect a strategic business decision by Disney rather than an anticompetitive effect of the
        merger. Indeed, when considering the overall number of film releases (rather than just
          theatrical  releases), Disney’s output increased by 10% in the post-merger period

6.4.3.1.2.2.   Shortening of theatrical windows
(237)   During its investigation, the Commission received complaints from cinemas on the
         potential impact of the Transaction on the diversity of films available to European
        audiences. According to UNIC, the merged entity would be incentivised to reduce the
        length of the theatrical window. (269)
(238)   The Commission considers it unlikely that the merged entity would shorten the length of
         the theatrical window of  its films, in essence for two reasons.  First, the market
         investigation has indicated that the commercial success of a film in cinemas is crucial to
           its subsequent success in the audiovisual value chain. (270). A shortening of the theatrical
       window is therefore likely to negatively impact the commercial success of films in
        cinemas. Second, the strategy and/or statements of all other major US studios confirm
         that a shortening of the theatrical window does not make economic sense. Disney has
        explained that its films are often subject to a theatrical window of at least 45 days. (271)
         Further, public sources referred to by the Notifying Party indicate that Universal is in the
        process of extending the theatrical window for its films to approximately 45 days in 2027,
       and that Sony is a vocal proponent of longer windows. (272) The Notifying Party also
        explained that Universal experimented with shorter windows but concluded that this was
         unprofitable and reverted to longer windows. (273)

         potential impact of the Transaction on the diversity of films available to European

         original and mid-budget productions. (274) UNIC noted that the financial incentives
         resulting from the Transaction, including the need to realise efficiencies, would likely
        reduce the merged entity’s appetite for creative risk-taking. (275)

6.4.3.1.3     Conclusion
(245)   For all the above reasons, the Commission concludes that the Transaction does not raise

6.4.3.2.2     UIP Countries
(265)   The Commission has undertaken a further competitive assessment in the countries where
       UIP is active (‘UIP Countries’) (301) and the EEA Member States where UIP is not
         active (‘Non-UIP Countries’) (302). This is because in the UIP Countries, film portfolios
         of Paramount and Universal are already distributed together through UIP OpCos and UIP
        Shared Licensees. (303) In the UIP Countries, by virtue of UIP, there are also structural
         links between Paramount and Universal, which are not present in the Non-UIP Countries.
(266)   The Commission’s assessment of  this market has therefore focused on what the
         implications of the addition of Warner’s portfolio to the merged entity would be,
         distinguishing between the countries in which the portfolios of Paramount, Warner, and
        Universal would be distributed together (UIP Countries) from those in which their
         respective  portfolios would be  distributed  separately (Non-UIP  Countries). The
        Notifying Party has also provided its views for both groups of countries separately.

6.4.3.2.2.1.   Notifying Party’ views
(267)   The Notifying Party submits that the Transaction does not raise concerns either in
         countries where Paramount films are distributed through UIP or a UIP licensee.

(269)   Second, the Notifying Party submits that, when looking at the right market, UIP’s share
        remains below 25% in all five countries except Poland ([20-30]%), and even combining

        a third-party studio – i.e., [third-party studio]. (305)

6.4.3.2.3     Non-UIP Countries

6.4.3.2.3.1.   Notifying Party’ views
(295)   The Notifying Party submits that the merged entity will be incentivized to (i) maintain
          their existing distribution local offices in the Non-UIP EEA countries where local offices
        already exist, and (ii) shift to self-distribution in the Non-UIP EEA countries where the
         larger slate and associated local box office would justify this commercial decision.
(296)    Firstly, it would not be economically rational, absent territory-specific countervailing
          factors, to add costly layers of intermediation in territories where Warner already has its
      own distribution office, and where the merger increases the volume of titles over which
         fixed costs involved in distribution and marketing can be spread. The merged entity is
         clearly incentivized to distribute their planned larger combined slate by relying on its
      own local offices, as the costs of a local office (which are mostly fixed) ought to be even
        lower given the merged entity’s planned larger slate, enabling it to enjoy the benefits of
         self-distribution at lower cost (on a per film basis).
(297)   Secondly, the Notifying Party submits that self-distribution aligns economic incentives
       between the producer and cinemas. The incentives of producers to maximise box office
        performance are enhanced because of the importance of theatrical performance in
        subsequent windows. This incentive does not apply to third-party distributors who only
         distribute theatrically for studios. On the other hand, third-party distributors may have
         conflicting incentives, particularly where third-party distributors own a stake in local
        cinemas, as they also have an incentive to monetise their downstream exhibition business.
(298)   Thirdly, the Notifying Party submits that self-distribution also ensures that marketing and
         distribution activities are focused on maximizing the performance of the producer’s own
           titles. Where a third-party distributor acts on behalf of multiple producers, contractual
         protections to do the best for each individual film can mitigate conflicts, but they cannot
         eliminate all practical allocation issues, particularly where the distributor must prioritize
        resources across competing titles. The distributor may therefore need to act in the interest
        of one studio’s film over another studio’s film.
(299)    Finally, the Notifying Party submits that for the Non-UIP EEA countries where neither
       Paramount nor Warner currently have a local office (namely Austria and Malta), the
       merged entity will internally assess whether the benefits of self-distribution will justify
         the (fixed) costs of setting up and running a local office. As the costs of a local office
         will be spread over its larger combined slate of 30+ films per year, the Combined Entity
         will have more incentives to set up a local office compared to the pre-Transaction
         scenario. (332)

6.4.4.   The theatrical distribution value chain - Assessment of coordinated effects

6.4.4.1. Introduction
(311)   The Commission also assessed whether the Transaction would give rise to coordinated
         effects on the market for the distribution of US films for theatrical release.
(312)   Most cinemas that responded to the market investigation submitted that the Transaction
       would make it possible, easier and/or more likely for some or all film distributors to
        coordinate   (i.e.,   align)   their  commercial   strategies  towards  cinemas/cinema
         operators. (338)
(313)    First, as regards the possible terms of coordination, respondents have pointed to rental
         rates (fee splits), length of theatrical release window, release date scheduling and screen
         allocation, the  latter covering aspects such as minimum screen commitments and

6.4.4.3.1      Possible terms of coordination

(329)    First, as regards release date scheduling, the Commission notes that this is a pre-existing

        reduction in) film output. However, for the reasons set out above at Section 6.4.3.1.2.1

         that coordination would arise to reduce the length of the theatrical release window or

(335)   The Commission’s assessment of the sustainability of coordination on rental fees and

           (i) whether the coordinating firms are able to reach a mutual understanding on the terms

          rivals but also customers) are not in a position to disrupt the coordination.
(336)  On the likelihood of coordination, the Commission considers that the reduction from five
         to four US major film studios as a result of the Transaction could potentially be
        considered as an element facilitating coordination on screen allocation and/or rental fees
         since the fewer the number of remaining firms in a market, the easier, in principle, it is
         to find and/or maintain a consensus, whilst at the same time reducing the alternatives
         available to cinema operators.
(337)   The Commission also considered whether contact between major US studios across
        multiple EEA jurisdictions or adjacent segments of the audiovisual value chain could
          facilitate coordination. However, the two terms identified in this Section (rental fees and
        screen allocation) are negotiated bilaterally, on a national basis, and are confidential
       between the contracting  parties. Contact between the major US studios in other
         jurisdictions or segments therefore does not materially increase the risk of coordination
       on those terms.
(338)   The Commission notes the submission by most cinemas that shared distribution of more
        than one major’s films can ease the standardisation of terms. In the EEA the only such
        arrangement is UIP; as discussed in Section 7.4, the Final Commitments provide for
        Paramount’s complete exit from UIP in the EEA and interim ring-fencing measures,
        including on rental rates and booking terms. Post-Transaction the merged entity’s films
         will no longer be co-distributed with films of another US major studio through a shared
          distributor. This reinforces the conclusion that coordination would not be sustainable.
(339)   The Commission considers whether the terms of coordination can be sufficiently
        monitored. As regards the screen allocation: while commitments regarding screen
         allocation are negotiated bilaterally between a studio/ distributor and cinema, the number
         of screens and showtimes actually allocated to a given film is to a significant extent
        observable, albeit not in a centralised manner, for example by consulting the websites of
         the various cinema operators on a weekly basis. The Commission notes, however, that
       what is observable is the allocation actually implemented, rather than the minimum
        screen or showtime commitments agreed bilaterally between a studio and a cinema.
(340)  As regards the rental fees, while the approximate range of revenue splits is broadly
       known, the exact split of the rental fee negotiated between distributors and cinemas is
        not public and is commercially sensitive. (355) This applies to both rental splits agreed on
        a film-by-film basis (as is generally the case with smaller cinemas) and to pre-arranged
         rental splits agreed across one of the Parties’ entire film portfolio and for a duration that
         generally exceeds one year (as is the case with various large cinema chains). (356) This

(342)   The Commission has considered whether any possible retaliation mechanism could make
         sustainable any potential coordinated behaviour among the major US studios. Such
       mechanisms could  theoretically  consist  of a temporary  returning  to competitive
        behaviour on the terms in question. However, rental fees and screen allocation are
        negotiated bilaterally and confidentially between each studio and each cinema. A studio
        wishing to punish a deviating studio by worsening its own terms would therefore not be
        able to signal to the deviating studio that it is doing so in retaliation, nor to target the
        punishment at the deviating studio: it could only worsen its terms vis-à-vis cinemas
         generally, at a cost to itself and without any assurance that the deviating studio would
        perceive the response as punishment.
(343)   The only credible retaliation mechanism the Commission identified is that of one or
         several major US studios scheduling the release of one or more of their high-potential
         films at the same time as that of the deviating major US studio, to hurt the latter’s
        revenues. Such a mechanism would not, however, deter deviation. In releasing a high-
         potential film against another, the retaliating studio would significantly hurt its own
        revenues through audience cannibalisation, and a threat deters only if the deviating firm
        expects it to be carried out. Moreover, the mechanism operates on a different parameter
       from that on which coordination is assumed to take place and could not be targeted at the
         specific cinemas or terms in respect of which deviation occurred. This finding does not
       depend on the term on which coordination is assumed: the absence of a credible deterrent
         applies equally to any possible tacit understanding on release date scheduling, the length
        of the theatrical release window or film output.

         films were to become less favourable. (358)

6.4.4.4. Conclusion
(347)   The Commission considers that the Transaction does not raise serious doubts as to its
         compatibility with the internal market as a result of horizontal coordinated effects on the
        market for the distribution of US films for theatrical release.
(348)   The Commission considers coordination unlikely on release dates, shortened theatrical
       windows or film output. Release-date scheduling is demand-expanding, shorter windows
       would conflict with rivals’ commercial interests, and there is no reliable basis for
        concluding that a reduction in output would be in the combined entity’s interest.
(349)  As regards rental fees and screen allocation, any possible coordination would in any event
        not be sustainable. The Commission has identified no credible mechanism by which the
        major US studios could deter deviation from any tacitly agreed terms, which is sufficient
       on its own to render such coordination unsustainable. In addition, as regards rental fees,
         the ability of the major US studios to detect deviation from any tacitly agreed split would
        be considerably limited, given that the negotiated terms are non-public and commercially
         sensitive.

6.4.5.2. Wholesale supply of TV channels

6.4.5.2.1     Wholesale supply of children’s pay TV channels

6.4.5.2.1.1.   The Notifying Party’s views
(380)   The Notifying Party submits that the horizontal overlap between Paramount and Warner
       on the market for the wholesale supply of children’s pay TV channels will not lead to
       any competition concerns at the EEA or national level for the following reasons.
(381)    First, across the EEA, children’s viewing of dedicated children’s pay TV channels is in
        steady and significant decline as viewers shift at scale to other viewing alternatives,
        mainly SVOD  platforms  and  other VOD  services. Competitive  pressure  from
     SVOD/VOD offerings is particularly high in the children’s segment. Nowadays, only a
        very small percentage of children’s content is viewed on dedicated children’s pay TV
        channels. Most children’s content is viewed on SVOD platforms (such as Netflix,
       Disney+ or Amazon Prime Video) and on YouTube. SVOD services and YouTube carry
        a large amount of children’s content including the same or similar titles to those available
       on linear pay TV channels. Therefore, such services are in direct competition with linear
       pay TV for children’s viewership. (406)
(382)   The move in audiences away from children’s pay TV is consistent with drops in
        viewership, revenues and profitability of children’s pay TV channels. Such drops overlap
        with steep increases in the viewership of children’s content on SVOD and YouTube. (407)
(383)   This structural decline of linear children’s pay TV constrains channel suppliers and
        precludes any attempt by the merged entity to leverage its combined children’s channel
         portfolio to extract more favourable terms from European retail TV distributors/MVPDs
         post-Transaction. (408)
(384)   Second, households across the EEA can access highly substitutable children’s content on
      FTA TV channels, which often offer the exact same shows and programming as on pay
       TV. Given the broad duplication in content, pay TV and FTA TV channels compete for
         the same audiences, with FTA TV children’s channels often even outperforming pay TV
         children’s channels in viewership. As such, post-Transaction the Parties’ activities in the
        wholesale supply of children’s pay TV channels will also be constrained by a large
       number of leading suppliers of children’s FTA TV programming (including Super RTL,
       KiKA, RAI, NPO Clan, Gulli, France 5, TF1, TVP ABC, and RTP2). (409)


         the new regulation on programming and investment obligations for European works and works by
        independent producers, given the entry into force of Legislative Decree 208/2021 containing the new
        Consolidated Law on Audiovisual Media Services.

(386)   Fourth,  wholesale  suppliers  of TV  channels  typically  negotiate  with  retail TV

        a bouquet of channels) rather than on a channel-by-channel basis, or on a genre-by-genre

(387)   Children’s pay TV channels are not a driver of pay TV subscriptions (not least because
         subscription decisions are made by adults, not the children who view the content in
         question) and therefore are not an important component of retail TV packages. There is
        a direct correlation between the consumer demand for a particular channel or service (i.e.,
       consumer demand  for  children’s TV has  fallen  dramatically) and  the MVPDs’
         willingness to pay for it and include it in its bouquet (i.e., MVPDs are less willing to pay
         for children’s TV channels). This dynamic ensures that the Transaction cannot result in
       an increased bargaining power for the Parties in the wholesale supply of children’s pay
     TV channels which would theoretically allow them to impose less favourable conditions
       on their MVPD customers post-Transaction. (412)
(388)    Fifth, MVPDs are large and sophisticated buyers with substantial countervailing buyer
        power.  Importantly,  the wide range  of  alternative sources  of  children’s  content
         strengthens MVPDs’ bargaining power in their negotiations with TV channel suppliers.
     MVPDs can and do incorporate a wide array of children’s content (extending beyond
         linear pay TV channels) directly into their own retail packages – most obviously FTA
     TV channels, but also Disney+, YouTube, Netflix, Amazon Prime Video, and other
        streaming platforms – either as parts of bundles or as add-ons. The availability of these
        commercially viable alternatives provides MVPDs with meaningful optionality in
         negotiations with suppliers of children’s pay TV channels and has, in practice, enabled
       them to exert pricing discipline when agreeing carriage terms for children’s channels. In
       view if this, post-Transaction, the merged entity will lack the ability or incentive to raise
         prices or worsen terms to European MVPDs. (413)

6.4.5.2.2     Wholesale supply of pay TV channels
(412)  As set out in Section 6.3, the Parties have horizontally overlapping activities that give
          rise to affected markets in the potential market for the wholesale supply of pay TV
        channels in Ireland and Poland.

6.4.5.2.2.1.   The Notifying Party’s views
(413)    First, the Notifying Party submits that the Parties’ combined shares in the potential
        markets for the wholesale supply of pay TV channels in Ireland and Poland are modest,
        with limited increments.
(414)   In Ireland, the Parties’ combined share in 2024 was [20-30]%, with an increment of
       [5-10]% (from Paramount). Paramount’s market share has since decreased, as Paramount
        discontinued four pay TV channels as of 31 December 2025. Excluding these pay TV
        channels from the 2024 market share estimates would bring the increment down to
        [5-10]%, with a combined share at [20-30]%. (438)
(415)   In Poland, the Parties’ combined share in 2024 was [30-40]%, with a limited increment
         of [5-10]% from Paramount. The increment has  since decreased, as Paramount
        discontinued seven channels as of 31 December 2025. Excluding these pay TV channels
       from the 2024 market share estimates would bring the increment down to [0-5]%, with a
       combined share at [30-40]%. (439)
(416)   Second, the Notifying Party notes that the merged entity will continue facing strong
        competition post-Transaction.
(417)   The market for linear TV channels has undergone a marked structural decline in recent
         years, driven by the rapid growth of SVOD and other non-linear services. The popularity
         of linear TV is in sustained decline as end-customers shift to other viewing non-linear
         alternatives, mainly SVOD services. In response, linear TV providers – including
       Paramount in both Ireland and Poland – are gradually discontinuing their TV channels or
         consolidating their feeds across multiple countries. In this landscape, SVOD services act
        as strong competitive constraint on pay TV channels in Ireland and Poland. Thus, any
        attempt to worsen competitive conditions for the supply of pay TV channels post-
        Transaction would only serve to accelerate that trend. (440)
(418)   In addition to SVOD, the merged entity will continue facing competitive constraints from
        a range of pay TV channel suppliers, including: Polsat, TVP, Disney, Canal+, Kino
        Polska TV, Antenna and IKO Media Group in Poland; Sky and Disney in Ireland. (441)
(419)   Furthermore, the Parties’ pay TV channels will continue to be competitively constrained
       by FTA TV channel suppliers. FTA TV channels are widely carried across retail TV
        distributor’s/MVPDs’ bundles and offer similar content to the content available on

6.5.     Vertical effects

6.5.1.   Legal framework
(495)   According  to  the  Non-Horizontal  Guidelines,  (515)  non-coordinated  effects may
         significantly impede effective competition as a result of a vertical merger if such merger
        gives rise to foreclosure. Foreclosure occurs where actual or potential competitors’ access
         to supplies or markets is hampered or eliminated as a result of the merger, thereby



(514)    Form CO, paragraphs 1644-46.
(515)    Non-Horizontal Guidelines, pages 6-25.
                                                            102

reducing those companies’ ability and/or incentive to compete. (516) Such foreclosure
      may discourage entry or expansion of competitors or encourage their exit. (517)
(496)   The Non-Horizontal Guidelines distinguish between two forms of foreclosure. First,
         input foreclosure occurs where the merger is likely to raise the costs of downstream
        competitors by restricting their access to an important input. (518) Foreclosure may also
        take more subtle forms, such as the degradation of the quality of input supplied. In its
        assessment, the Commission may consider a series of alternative or complementary
         possible strategies. (519) Second, customer foreclosure occurs where the merger is likely
         to foreclose upstream competitors by restricting their access to a sufficient customer
         base. (520)
(497)   In assessing the likelihood of an anticompetitive foreclosure scenario, the Commission
        examines,  first, whether the merged entity would have, post-merger, the ability to
         substantially foreclose access to inputs or customers; second, whether it would have the
         incentive to do so; and third, whether a foreclosure strategy would have a significant
         detrimental effect on competition. In practice, these factors are often examined together
        as they are closely intertwined. (521)
(498)   Pursuant to Article 2(2) of the Merger Regulation, a concentration which would not
         significantly impede effective competition, in the internal market or in a substantial part
         of  it, shall be declared compatible with the internal market. Conversely, pursuant to
         Article 2(3) of the Merger Regulation, a concentration which would significantly impede
         effective competition, in the internal market or in a substantial part of it, shall be declared
        incompatible with the internal market. In that regard, it is sufficient for the Commission
         to establish that the Transaction is likely to lead to a significant impediment of effective
        competition.
